Before the House rose, I pointed out that the two grounds upon which hon. gentlemen opposite seek to refuse this investigation were not substantial, and, upon the testimony of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and statements made by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), ought not to prevail. It is quite true, the Prime Minister, since making these statements, and for reasons which are obvious to all within the sound of my voice, endeavoured to repudiate to some extent the meaning taken from the statement he made. I understand that the Finance Minister is to follow ine in this debate, and it will not surprise me should he make an effort to show that when he made the statement that Canada was to pay her full share for participation in the war, he did not mean what he said.
I cannot conceive that any other course is open to the Solicitor General than to support the resolution of my right hon. leader. I pointed out before six o'clock that when he spoke in the debate on the Address he said that if the Shell Committee were appointed by this Government this Government would hold itself responsible for the conduct of that committee. I have proved that the committee was appointed by this Government and that it has expended money belonging to the taxpayers of Canada. Therefore, after the statement made by the Solicitor General, he must, to be consistent and to be honest with himself, support this resolution. The last special plea filed against the resolution was that filed by the Solicitor General, and, as was to be expected, it is the most technical plea of all. The defence made by the Solicitor General, in his speech following that of the hon. member for St. John, was based upon a plea of demurrer. Demurrer, as those of us who belong to the legal profession know, is a most technical pleading which has been abolished in most of the provinces in this 
Dominion. It is to the effect that when a claim is made, although the defendant agrees as to the equity of the claim, nevertheless, on account of some inaccuracy or of some inexactitude as to the description of the claim, the date, or circumstances, in the plaintiff's allegation, it ought not to prevail, but should be ruled out of court on account of these technicalities. As I said, this plea has been abolished in the several courts of Nova Scotia and in other provinces of Canada. But sometimes the plea is made in the police court. I have known myself that when a criminal is put on trial and is defended by a young and inexperienced lawyer, if the court before which the trial is held is not presumed to be as well grounded in the principles of law as the judges in the higher courts, the lawyer defending him takes advantage of the fact, and, although the criminal is proved to have committed the offence, if the evidence shows for instance, that instead of it having been committed at 9 o'clock in the morning it was committed at midnight, he argues that therefore the criminal is entitled to an acquittal. The whole answer of the Solicitor General to the demands of the right hon. leader of the Opposition for an inquiry into the purchase of shells and other munitions, is that the statement made by the hon. member for Carleton as to the quantities and deliveries of shells and fuses, as well as the particulars of claim in other respects, were not absolutely accurate, and therefore the resolution of my right hon. leader should not be accepted by the House. In effect, the Solicitor General says that, inasmuch as the member for Carleton did not state these particulars correctly, no matter how many millions may have been lost by the incompetency of the members of the Shell Committee and the dishonesty of some of those with whom they did business, no inquiry is to be made and no restitution ordered. The hon. member for Calgary stated that Mr. Thomas and Mr. Hichens and Mr. Kerr said to the Prime Minister that the prices had in some instances been high, but acquitted the gentleman presiding over the Shell Committee of any wrongful purpose. I should like to ask the member for Calgary how a baby can be convicted of any wrongful purpose. The Minister of Militia and Defence said that the Shell Committee was a mere baby created by him. I presume his description of the majority of the Shell Committee was an exact description. So it comes down to this, that while the Shell Committee, on

account of incompetence or for some other reason, may have committed the offences charged against it, nevertheless they ought to be acquitted of any wrongful act. It is a well-known principle of law that if a man places in the hands of an infant a weapon or instrument that is dangerous, and in the handling of that weapon or instrument the infant causes damage, the baby is not nut upon his trial for the act. Who is held responsible by the court? The party who placed the dangerous weapon in the hands of the infant. Therefore, if the Shell Committee is a mere infant, as described by the Minister of Militia and Defence, who is to be held responsible for the wrongs which it has committed? Why, it must be the patty who gave the opportunity to the baby to do those things which have resulted in loss to the people of Canada. The above advance payment being made for the purpose of enabling the company to finance the contract.

citor General, although I am not sure-said that we were going to investigate a corpse. Yet one and all are agreed to have an investigation after the war, when the corpse will have become completely decomposed. It is a corpse; vote against the inquiry, say they, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite are willing to inquire into the corpse Wo years afterwards. The cry is:	Delay, delay,
delay, and to what end? To enable Col, J. W. Allison to flee away into some far country with which Canada has no extradition treaty. Delay until the grave closes over the remains of some of the principal actors in this grim tragedy. Delay until records and documents are lost and perhaps destroyed and the proof of the charges rendered difficult, if not impossible! Delay to enable 'Col. Allison and his fellow bandits to make more millions out of the blood and agony of Canada and thfe Empire while they increase the peril of both!
There is another point, however in the speech made by the hon. member for Car-leton, another ground for accusation, and that is in regard to prices. The hon. member for 'Carleton found fault not only as to nondeliveries, but as to the prices being exorbitant and altogether unjustifiable. Not one hon. gentleman sitting opposite to me has ventured for a moment to defend the prices. That charge is absolutely undefended up to the present moment. By their silence, they have admitted that the statements made by he hon. member for Carleton as regards the exorbitant character of the prices are absolutely just and true and indefensible.
I would have no great fault to find with the contracts g.iven to the United States when the war first broke out, because the cry was for shells, and more shells. If we could not manufacture the shells in Canada, then the Shell Committee had a right to go to the United States, but did the Shell Committee make contracts with companies making fuses? No, they made contracts with middlemen, with mushroom companies, which divided up not only the profits but the advances that had been made to them by the Shell Committtee. The Shell Committee advanced to these people over $3,000,000, and we know that that amount was given them, they dllege, ' for the purpose of equipping factories. Now, $3,000,000 would be enough to equip ten fuse factories in Canada; for, as I am advised, $300,000 will equip one fuse factory equal in capacity to that now operated by 
the Russell Motor Car 'Company. What would that mean? It would mean ten fuse factories carried on in Canada and the expenditure of money among our own people. Have we hard times in Canada? Is there unemployment? I read only the other day of a case in Ottawa of four families huddled together in a shack, mother and children practically dying of hunger because the father had no employment. Under the very shadow of the Parliament Buildings this condition of affairs exists. Yet contracts for fuses, and advances to equip fuse factories, are given to Colonel Allison and his friends, and they hike off to the United States to spend the money. What does the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) say to that? Surely he is interested in labour problems. If he is interested in anything at all, he must he interested in the question of unemployment. Does he justify the advancing of this $3,000,000 to equip fuse factories in the United States, while men are walking the streets of Ottawa unemployed, and women and infants are dying of starvation in this capital of Canada? What about the city of Montreal? What about the city of Toronto? What about other cities in Canada? The equipping of ten fuse factories, the money for which was given to Col. Allison and his associates, would have given employment and prosperity, food and clothing and comforts, to hundreds of people in this country.
I had not intended to read any newspaper reports, but as my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) read an article from a newspaper published in Nova Scotia, in which the editor professes to believe that there is nothing in the charges, I shall quote from a newspaper published a g9od deal nearer to Ottawa and to the scene of Col. Allison's operations. I read from the Montreal Star, a thick and thin supporter of this Government:
The Shell Committee Charges.
Charges of the gravity of those which Dr. Pugsley has made against the late Shell Committee should not be allowed to remain as the mere casual remarks of a debater on the speech from the Throne. So old a Parliamentarian as. Dr. Pugsley knows that there is a proper way to bring statements of this sort before the House. And doubtless he will make good his accusations by some such formal step before the session is very much older.
In any case, the Government cannot permit these shocking and humiliating charges to remain uninvestigated. We are confident that no Canadian Government will hide behind the technicality that the money, said to be worse than wasted, was British money, entrusted to us to be carefully spent amidst the strain of a great war, and not our own money. That would be

to confess and proclaim that we would be less honest in dealing with sacred trust funds than in handling our personal property.
If a pound of British money, entrusted to a Canadian committee to buy the greatest possible amount of war material, was allowed to be diverted to Canadian private purses in inordinate profits, then the men guilty of this sordid and despicable treason were guility of weakening by just so much the fighting forces of the Empire in the face of an appalling peril. They might as well have gone to the trenches and taken the rifles out of the hands of our boys, fronting a German attack, and then sold these rifles for their personal profit to the first second-hand dealer whom they met. If this has been done, the country. wants to know it, regardless of the legal technically or partisan politics.
A thorough investigation into this whole shell game should be set on foot at once.
Mr. Speaker, some forty-three years ago public opinion throughout Canada became aroused by rumours that the party in power had taken advantage the necessities of the country for railway construction to snake financial gains for themselves and their friends. The matter came up in Parliament and an investigation was asked for. The leader of the Government on behalf of himself and his party denied the charges. Delay was demanded and the inquiry was refused. The Opposition put its case before the people, through the newspapers and the public forum. When Parliament again met, on a motion of censure the Government was defeated, and thereafter hopelessly beaten at the polls. It is the fate of another Conservative Government to have grow out of its regime another scandal, which, on account of the enormous amount of money involved and the tremendous magnitude of the interests jeopardized, the Pacific Scandal fades before it as the light of the morning star fades before the effulgence of the rising sun.	*
Do hon. gentlemen think that public opinion has become so calloused in Canada that it will permit their friends to traffic in the necessities of the nation, and in munitions and supplies needed for defending our civilization, nay our very existence, when it annihilated a Government for trafficking in a railway charter? All that Canada asks at the present time is that the Government shall show, by granting the investigation asked for by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, that they are not shielding, protecting or supporting the acts which are the subject of these exposures, and will prevent the possibility of their continuance. If they refuse, the appeal taken from their decision to the Cana-144
dian people will come in due time, and they will render as decisive a condemnation of this Government's conduct as was given against the Government of the late Sir John A. Macdonald in 1873.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has spoken for some five hours-
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-some four or five hours, and he has traversed a very extended field. It seemed to me a curious thing that my hon. friend should feel himself called upon to devote so much time to extricating the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) from the distressing position in which he found himself after the speech of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). The distress on the part of the hon. member for Carleton was quite marked. He has not been quite himself .since the 9th of March. He sent out a S.O.S. call to the good wrecking tug, his friend from Richmond. He felt himself completely stranded, and judging from the effort made to-night, the case is a total wreck.
Before I take up the serious parts-or what I assume my hon. friend to have intended as the most serious parts-of the address to which we have just listened, I desire to deal briefly with some of his arguments and statements in reply to the Solicitor General. My hon. friend came to the rescue of the hon. member for Carleton. He felt it was a case that needed his best assistance and, to do him. justice, I must say that he did reasonably well.

Thank you.
Hear, hear.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. He realized that he could only support fundamentally false statements by adding to them. He stood before this House to-night and, in the statements which he placed upon Hansard, he corroborated in every detail the statements made by the Solicitor General in answer to the hon.. member for Carleton. The hon. member for Carleton, in his speech the other night, in order to prove that the Shell Committee in giving these contracts had been actuated by considerations of political patronage, dwelt upon the fact that certain companies in this country had received no orders. He said: "Why has not the Dominion Iron and Steel Company received orders." And when the Solicitor General had pointed out that the



Dominion Iron; and Steel Company -had received orders-, then the apologist for the hon. member' for Carleton, the hon. member for Richmond, to-night says: Oh, the hon. member for Carleton was dealing with orders for shells. And yet it is a fact, it is on record in Hansard, that the hon. member for Carleton, in stating that the contracts that had been given to the Nova Scotia Steel -Company, referred to blanks, referred to discs, referred to plates, referred to numerous items not embraced under the term " shells." The great majority, in fact, were orders not for shells but for steel, or for parts of shells. My hon. friend referred to certain orders which had been given by the Shell Committee to companies doing business in the West. I want to direct the attention of the House to the argument of the hon. member for Carleton, when he was dealing with these questions. He said, as reported on page 1628 of Hansard:
No big orders were given for these-this is where the political part of It comes in. The Dominion Bridge Company got an order for 600,000, and the Canadian Westinghouse Company an order for 400,000. Outside of these, no big orders were given until you come down to the political end of it. I am not going into a long dissertation upon these transactions, but will merely point out some things which will interest my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. B. B. Bennett). I find that the Dominion Harvester Company, of Medicine Hat, were able to get an order for 10,000, and up to a month ago they had not delivered a single shell. The International Supply Company, of Medicine Hat, got an order for 10,000, and not a shell has been delivered. The Manitoba Bridge and Iron Works, of Winnipeg, got an order .for 20,000, and not a shell has been delivered.
Mr. Hanna: What is the date of those orders?
Mr. Carvell: I could not say exactly; it was during the summer of 1915. I am only giving these to show the political end of the transaction.
Now, what was the hon. member for Carleton attempting to establish? He was attempting to establish this, that this Shell Committee, fo-r political considerations, had given the orders to these companies in question, and he stated that these orders had been given some time in- the summer ot 1915. Now, what are the facts? The facts are precisely as stated by the Solicitor General, and, as a matter of fact, by the' hon. member for Richmond to-day. Take the case of the Dominion Harvester Company. Why, instead of that company having been given -an order by the Shell Committee for political purposes, they did not receive the order which was spoken of by the -hon. member for Carleton [Bir Thomas While.]
until January 12, 1916, after( the Shell Committee had become extinct. The order given to the Dominion Harvester Company upon the date given by the Solicitor General, January 12, 1916, for 10,000 shells, was given by the Imperial Munitions Board with which hon. gentlemen opposite find, absolutely no fault. The same statement can be made with regard to the order given to the International Supply Company on January 12, 1916. The same statement can be made with regard to th-e contracts given to the Manitoba Bridge and Iron Wo-rks, to the Medicine Hat Pump -and Brake Company, and to -the Manitoba Shell Company, and to all the other companies mentioned by the Solicitor General. It is 'a fact that shells were delivered by two of those companies but they were delivered on orders given previously to the date mentioned by the Solicitor General. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Richmond has corroborated in every particular the statements made by the Solicitor General in this House in his reply to the hon. member for Carleton. The fact of the matter is that the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), in order to bolster up a case against the Shell Committee, made a series of misrepresentations, I do not say wilful misrepresentations, to this House, -and when the Solicitor General met and answered the misrepresentations so made, the hon. member for Carleton felt himself called upon to -summon the hon. member for Richmond to his assistance, and to-night, as I stated, that hon. gentleman has attempted to bolster up the misstatements of the hon. member foT Carleton by further mis-statements, because only in that way could his course have been accounted for.
Some matters have been dealt with by the hon. member for Richmond to which I desire briefly to call attention. He referred to an Order in Council presented before the Davidson Commission. He said that Order in Council gave -authority to Allison, as I understood him, to purchase revolvers. The Order in Council gave authority to the Minister of Militia to purchase 1,000 automatic pistols. The name of Allison was not mentioned in the Order in -Council. He stated that the Government had paid a commission of $4.50 up-o-n every Colts revolver. That is an absolute mis-statement of fact. The Government of Canada did not pay $4.50 commission upon each -Colts revolver; the Government of Canada did not pay one cent commission upon the purchases of -Colts revolvers. The -Government- of Canada

obtained 'Colts revolvers at precisely the same rate as any Government-outside of the Government of the United States, which has a special arrangement-pays for Colt revolvers. The statement, therefore, is absolutely inaccurate. My hon. friend has referred to perjury before the Davidson Commission. I think it might 'be well to await the report of that commission; but if my hon. friend is too impatient to await that report, I think he owes it to himself and to this House, if he desires prosecution, to- lay an information against the party complained of; and if he lays a complaint and the matter comes before the Department of Justice, in the usual course, for extradition, the Department of Justice will do its duty, as in all similar cases.
My hon. friend referred to Yoakum, Lignanti and Allison. All I have to say is that he evidently knows these gentlemen better than we do, because until this night I never heard of Lignanti and Yoakum, and so far as Allison is concerned, I have heard his name but I have never seen him or spoken to him, and I believe the same can 'be said of all the other members of the Government sitting here to-night, or most of them.
The Minister of Militia also?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Militia has stated that he is acquainted with Allison.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, after speaking for some hours here to-night, wondered if he was making any impression upon this House. Well, I will tell you how he could make an impression upon this House. If h^ will bring home to any membeT of the Shell Committee, or any member of this Government a charge of corruption or of dishonesty, or of dishonour, he will make an impression on this House and on the country. But he has not done so, Mr. Speaker, nor has he laid a foundation for it. There is not an hon. gentleman from the leader of the Opposition down who has dared to state that Alexander Bertram is a dishonest man. No one has dared to state so far that Col. Carnegie is a dishonest man. No one has impeached the integrity of Col. Cantley; he has been spoken of in terms of eulogy by hon. gentlemen opposite. No one has made a charge against any member of the Shell Committee, and no hon. member who
has spoken in this debate has made a charge against the honour, the probity or the integrity of any member of this Government.
The hon. member for Richmond has had a good deal to say about the Solicitor General. He stated in that connection that the Solicitor General likes to speak last. Well, I will say this for the Solicitor General- and I think it will be admitted to be true by all members of this House-that when he is on his feet he does not decline to answer questions, he is never unprepared to say: I am making this statement now; what have you to say in contradiction of it-and say it now if you want to? The hon. member for Richmond, attacking the Solicitor General, declined to allow the Solicitor General to ask him pertinent and relevant questions with regard to the matter which he was bringing to the attention of the House. Whatever may be said about the Solicitor General, it cannot be said that he lacks courage when he is upon his feet.
The hon. member for Carleton, following the right hon. leader of the Opposition, started out to prove that this Shell Committee had exercised favouritism in the placing of contracts. The hon. Solicitor General challenged him to name Conservative firms who had received contracts, saying that he would mention Liberal firms,'name for name-and that challenge remains unanswered. The hon. member for Carleton stated that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company received no orders. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company received orders to the amount oi over $5,000,000. The hon. member for Carleton said that the Canadian General Electric Company received no orders. As a matter of fact the Canadian General Electric Company received orders to the extent of over $10,000,000. That has been shown here to-night, and it was shown by the Solicitor General in his speech. That, it is stated, is a mere 'technicality; but although the hon. member for Carleton started out to prove that the Canadian General Electric Company, for which he professes admiration, had been discriminated against, the facts are that the Canadian General Electric Company and its subsidiary company received orders aggregating over $10,000,000. So far as the statements of the hon. member for Carleton are concerned, they have been proved to be fundamentally false-I do not mean false to his knowledge, because I do not believe that the hon. member for Carleton put them forward as false to his knowledge. The hon. gentleman had a bad

brief; if he had been in court- he would have thrown up his brief; he would have been obliged to throw it up.
We have had a good deal of assertion and counter-assertion in this debate, and I purpose taking up the text of the resolution in order that we may see what the right hon. leader of the Opposition asks us to do. He has moved a resolution as follows:
That a special committe of members of this House be appointed to inquire into all purchases of shells or other munitions or goods by the Shell Committee formed by the Minister of Militia, as stated to this House by the Prime Minister on the 15th April, 1915, together with all contracts made or orders given by the said committee for any shells or other munitions or goods, with authority to the said committee to examine witnesses under oath and to require the production of any documents, books, letters or papers; and that such special committee be directed to report from time to time to this House in such manner as it may think advisable.
Mr. Speaker, this inquiry would involve disclosure of all purchases of goods and munitions by the committee. It would involve disclosure of all orders or contracts given or made by tb^e committee. It would involve disclosures of all letters, cables, telegrams and documents connected therewith. 1 contend that if this inquiry is had on the resolution of my right hon. friend, there must necessarily be disclosed all confidential communications by cable or otherwise passing between the War Office and the Shell Committee. It would reveal to the world, to friends and foes alike, the extent of the orders which had been placed in Canada, the resources of Canada, the present condition of all contracts placed by the Shell Committee in Canada. It would by inference-I do not think this is a farfetched argument-disclose to a certain extent the -strategy of the War Office, because it would disclose the needs of the War Office from time to time. It would disclose the character of the shells, the size of the shells, indicating the views of the War Office with regard to the campaign. It would reveal further the financial difficulties experienced by the Imperial Government in placing these orders in Canada. I know that my right hon. friend would be the last to suggest that information should be given which would be of relief or assistance to the enemy. But if the Kaiser himself desired to know what orders had been placed in Canada, the conditions concerning all contracts and the entire history of the dealings of the War Office with the Shell Committee, he could not take a more effectual method of accomplishing his tSir Thomas White.]
purpose than through an inquiry such as that suggested in this resolution.
The granting or the refusal of this resolution shopld depend upon some underlying principle. What is the issue before the House? The issue is whether this inquiry should be held or not. I desire to take up the reasons given by my right hon. friend in moving for this inquiry. He says that the Shell Committee is a committee of this Government. Mr. Speaker, there cannot be responsibility unless there is authority. It is true that this Shell Committee was named by this Government, but it is also true that this Shell Committee was agent of the Imperial Government. It acted under instructions from the Imperial Government; it had no authority to take any step or give any order unless with the approval or upon the instructions of the Imperial Government. This Government had the responsibility of naming the members and this Government, having named the members, the Shell Committee became the committee or the agent of the Imperial Government. My right hon. friend himself says that the names are Respectable names; he could not say otherwise. No member of this House could say that the names of the member? of the Shell Committee are not respectable names. This Government discharged its duty in naming the members of the committee but that does not alter the fact that the committee is a committee of the Imperial Government. I repeat that no charge has been made against the honour or integrity of any member of this committee or any member of the Government. This Shell Committee spent no Canadian money; not one dollar of Canadian money has been spent by it. Every dollar that has been spent by the Shell Committee has been Imperial money. The Dominion Government, from time to time, made advances to the Imperial Government, but the Canadian Government did not pay for the orders given by the Shell Committee. It has been stated that Canada will indirectly pay a portion of the expenditures by the Shell Committee because Canada is paying her full share of this war. I rejoice that Canada is paying her lull share of this war. Canada in 1899 did not pay her full share of the war. When I stated in the House to the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that Canada was paying her full share of this war I meant it, the Government meant it and the Government- meant it from the beginning. But that does not mean that

the Shell Committee has been spending any money of the Dominion Government. If it is argued that because Canada intends to pay ultimately to the Imperial Government a share of, the expenditure at the front that she cannot pay to-day, but which will be apportioned to her later, this Parliament is entitled to hold an investigation into the actions of the War Office, or the Minister of Munitions of the Imperial Government, then, it seems to me, it must follow on the same line of argument that this Parliament would be entitled to hold an investigation into all the orders placed by Great Britain in the United States, the United Kingdom or in any other country in the world. Does any one suggest that that would be feasible or possible or that this Parliament would have any right to do that? It seems to me that it is a farfetched argument for the purpose of giving this Parliament apparent jurisdiction to inquire into the transactions of the Shell Committee. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has stated that the Shell Committee was a branch of the Government.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
took a constituent, according to a statement made in this House, into the office of the Shell Committee and from what I can learn obtained a contract for him.
bir WILFRID LAURIER: Not a constituent of mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A friend?
A friend, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
took a friend into the office of the Shell Committee and succeeded in getting a contract for him. In order to meet the charge that this Shell Committee was made use of by this Government, I desire to say that I am a member of this Government and that I never set foot inside the Shell Committee's office from the day it was established to the day it became, defunct.
The Minister of Militia did if you did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister ol Militia exercised no authority over the Shell Committee.
You do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am speaking of myself. My hon. friend does not know.

Why do you say
that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: / My hon. friend says that he knows?
No, I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
How could the
Minister of Militia exercise authority over Col. Cantley or over Sir Alexander Bertram, against [DOT] whose integrity no charge whatever has been made?
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the Conservative candidate in my county made a direct charge reflecting on the integrity of General Bertram?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know
whether he did or not. '
He did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend make a charge against the integrity of General -Bertram or Col. Cantley?

I say that General Bertram dealt with contracts awarded by the Shell Committee for political purposes, that he so dealt with them in my county, and if necessary I am prepared to say so at length. I want to say that he and Mr. Carnegie let these nefarious contracts for the War Office in the United States through Col. Allison who has been exposed to-night. My hon. friend will require all his time to explain that, and he had better get down to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I notice that when the Nova Scotia Steel Company is under consideration my hon. friend sings a different tune. My bon. friend speaks about favouritism in the letting of contracts. Has he anything to say about the Nova Scotia Steel Company getting contracts to the extent of $15,000,000 ?
That has nothing to do with this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not complaining in regard to that, but the hon. gentleman h-as had not a word to say in regard to that particular question.

After the Shell Committee had been in existence for two or three months the whole work of awarding contracts was assumed by General Bertram and Mr. Carnegie, and General Bertram employed his son in dealing with the question. If the hon. gentleman wants me to address the House on t^hat question, I will take occasion to do so before the debate closes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If Col. Cantley was there he no doubt felt his responsibility and if General Bertram was allowed to let contracts it would seem that they all had confidence in General Bertram. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has referred to this committee as being a branch of the Government. What does Sir Alexander Bertram say about the matter? Sir Alexander Bertram is a man whose standing is high in the community.
I have never heard a word breathed against the integrity of Sir Alexander Bertram -What does he say about the relationship between. this Government and the Shell Committee? This is what he said before leaving, when he had to go away with his health shattered by reason of the attacks which had been made upon him:
There is nobody suffering but myself. There is nobody but myself who can be injured. The Government has nothing to do with these contracts. I had no interference and I believe that I awarded as many contracts to Liberals as to Conservatives.
That is what Sir Alexander Bertram says and the Tecord bears him out. I venture to say that he let more contracts to Liberals than to Conservatives, and that any charge in so far as political favouritism or the exercise of patronage in connection with the transactions of the Shell Committee is concerned is absolutely false and without foundation. My right hon. friend, in speaking in support of his resolution, said that the British troops needed munitions and he blamed the Shell Committee. 'The Shell. Committee was the agent of the British .Government in this country and he blamed it because the British troops needed munitions. Who had the placing of the orders to be forwarded for the British Army? The War 'Office. The Shell Committee was not a sovereign body' like a Government exercising its authority as to when it would buy ot what it would buy or the amount it would buy; it was simply the agent of the Imperial Government, taking instructions like any other agent and acting simply within the limits of its

authority. How did this committee originate? An order came for 200,000 empty shells to the Minister of Militia and it was suggested that he get them in the United States. At a time like that they were anxious to get munitions from any part of the world. The Minister of Militia called together some o-f the leading steel manufacturers of this country and one or two experts and said: Cannot we make these shells in Canada? That was the proper course for him to take. He called together the men he ought to have called together under .such circumstances. Whom else would he call together except the steel manufacturers, to see whether shells could be manufactured in Canada? On September 2 he has a conference, he has the experts present, they show the specifications, they explain the method of inspection and the Shell Committee is established.
The Shell Committee was established by the Minister of Militia for the purpose of obtaining munitions in Canada, and for the purpose of giving Canada the businesg. And there is just this to be said at this point. No matter what may be said against the Shell Committee, it is a fact that from that action taken by the Minister of Militia on September 2nd, 1914, there has grown in Canada the largest business in the British Empire, a total of no less than $500,000,000 worth of orders having been placed. It has been stated that the committee let contracts at high prices. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) admitted in his speech that the committee requested the War Office to authorize them to purchase at certain prices.
I think that is practically correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is to say,
that instead of the Shell Committee having authority to place orders in Canada at such prices as it might approve, they submitted the prices that it might approve, they submitted the offers to the Imperial Government, saying, "We can obtain such and such'a price. Do you approve?" Now, it is perfectly clear that if there was any shortage of munitions for the British troops in the field, the blame cannot be attributed to the Shell Committee, for the Shell Committee was not a free and independent sovereign body, exercising its own discretion and having its own money to spend, but a committee that made no move without the sanction and approval of the British Government.

I assume that my hon. friend believes that statement. Can he give us any evidence to substantiate it? The reason I ask is that the statement has been made on two or three occasions, but I have never seen any evidence to back it up. I am referring to the statement that the Shell Committee could not make any contracts without the sanction of the Imperial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that that is a fact.
We should like some evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is consistent with the w,hole course of dealings with the Shell Committee and the Imperial Government. The Imperial Government was paying every penny expended by the Shell Committee, and that is on record, in some pases at least. I believe it was the usual procedure of the Shell Committee to have the prices authorized by the Imperial Government, and then to place the orders. What does Alex. Bertram say about that? He says:
I have told you that after our first order the British War Office gave us further orders at prices fixed by themselves. When we sent quotations they stated that our prices were too high, and we accepted their prices. In passing I may say that nearly $20,000 surplus was turned back to the War Office on the first contract of 100,000 shells.
So it is perfectly clear the Shell Committee was acting under the direct authority cf the Imperial Government in placing these orders for munitions. How, then, can it be said that the Shell Committee was in any way responsible for a shortage of munitions at the front?
There is another feature which we might as well discuss at the present time. There is no doubt that it was necessary that fairly high prices should be offered in order to induce manufacturers to engage in the manufacture of shells. When this war broke out, how few realized or believed that it
would last two or three years. The common expectation was that it would be over in six months or a year. Manufacturers were naturally reluctant to go to the expense of installing the plant necessary to produce shells, and it was necessary to offer fairly high prices as an inducement. The British Government, as I have said, were placing orders all over the world, and would know prices. In this country plants were organized, machinery was installed, and orders were given in Canada by the Shell Committee to the amount of $500,000,000. Now, I think that is a very considerable amount to spend on munitions in Canada. When we consider the financial situation, and remember that Great Britain had to import gold, in some instances, in order.to pay for munitions in this country, I think it must be conceded that $500,000,000 is a very substantial amount of business to be placed by the Shell Committee in the country. There are some 400 manufacturers engaged in the business, and over 130,000 workmen employed, and it is all due to the establishment of the Shell Committee and the orders they gave under the instruction and direction of the Imperial Government. It has been stated that larger orders might have been given to Canada. Now, there is a financial side to this that is not generally understood, and I shall only touch upon it. The Imperial Government could raise abundance of money in New York, because New York is an international market, but a condition of their raising money in New York was that thoy should spend that money in the United States. It was not open to the Imperial Government to borrow money in New York, and then use that money outside of the United States for the purchase of munitions. That was illustrated in the Anglo-French loan. When the $500,000,000 loan was arranged, it was stipulated that the whole of the money should be expended in the purchase of American goods and supplies. Great Britain, in order to place the $500,000,000 worth of orders she has placed in Canada, was obliged in many instances to buy exchange in America at a cost of from three to five per cent, and in other cases, she was obliged to ship gold to this country in order to pay for the munitions ordefed through the Shell Committee. So, in dealing with the orders that have come to Canada, as compared or contrasted with those that have gone to the United States, the financial situation has to be borne in mind.

Now, what are the outstanding features of the Shell Committee's administration? They made mistakes; they have admitted that they made mistakes. In time of war all Governments, and all those charged with responsible duties, make mistakes. The conditions under which they worked rendered mistakes inevitable. Sir Alexander Bertram admits that the committee made mistakes. But it is a fact, as I have stated, that from small beginnings they built up the largest business in the British Empire, and I submit that, if they placed their orders with Canadian manufacturers, they are not responsible if there was delay in delivery. They placed their orders in accordance with their instructions from the British Government; they placed orders for empties; they placed orders for parts; there was difficulty in assembling and co-ordinating; but can the Shell Committee be fairly held responsible for delay in deliveries of orders given to responsible manufacturers? How can they be held responsible for the fact that the British Army had not munitions after the battle of the Marne? I think that has only to be stated to absolve the Shell Committee from any responsibility in that regard. We are in the advantageous position in considering this motion of having before us the fact of an investigation by experts of the War Office of the records of the Shell Committee. What do they say? Mr. Thomas says:
There is no suspicion whatever with regard to the Shell Committee.
And he speaks of the good faith, the honesty, the integrity of the members. He says:
Without doubt, they are honourable, honest, upright men.
He said that the committee had done excellent work under trying conditions and that General Bertram had placed the country under a debt of gratitude. He stated further that General Bertram worked like a Trojan day and night, and gave his services wjthout fee or reward, and he stated also, as I have mentioned already, that the biggest business in the British Empire to-day had been built up in twelve months. Mr. Thomas, whose name has been frequently mentioned by hon. gentlemen opposite, considered the criticism of Mr. Cantley and others unfair. He said that General Bertram was free from party bias and placed orders widely, not with two or three firms. According to the hon. member for Richmond, what should have been done is that orders should have been placed with two or three firms and that the hundreds of

manufacturing firms throughout Canada should have gone without orders at all. The work of the committee was satisfactory, not only to Thomas, hut to Hichens, to Brand, to the experts of the British War Office who were sent out here. I repeat, because I say it goes to the very root of this matter, that no charge of fraud, dishonesty nor corruption _has been put forward against the members of the Shell Committee.
We come now to the question: shall the inquiry be had? The committee is defunct and one would ask himself what purpose is served in bolding an investigation. We could not summon officials from the War Office. I do not believe that the War Office would consent to the pub-12	m.	lication of	confidential cablegrams and	other communications passing between them and the members o'f the Shell Committee. The hon. member for Carleton said: "Give me the committee and I will show you that the prices paid were higher than the prices paid in the United States and in England." How	could the hou.	member establish
what prices were paid by the Imperial Government in the United States and in England unless he summoned the Minister of Munitions or officials from the War Office? In my judgment, the Minister of Munitions or the officials of the War Office would not, at this time, submit to be put under examination as to the prices which they paid for shells and other munitions in the United Kingdom and in the United States. So, my hon. friend, if he had his committee, would not be able to establish what he hoped to establish, because they could not investigate the transactions of the British War Office, because the transactions of the Shell Committee are the transactions of the War Office and of no one else. They are not the transactions of this Government; this Government had no responsibility whatever as to prices nor as to the amount of orders which should be given. The responsibility lay with the Imperial Government, who gave the orders to the Shell Committee, and where there is no authority, there cannot be any responsibility. This Government had no authority whatever over the Shell Committee, and this Government, on no principle of Which I am aware, can be made responsible for the actions of the Shell Committee. I certainly decline to take responsibility for the actions of a committee over which I had absolutely no control whatsoever.
-MARCH 28, 1916
There is another feature of this question. Have we any right to investigate without the Imperial consent? If tlhe British War Office paid every penny of the money, as they have; if no order was placed except with their consent or upon their instructions, have we any right to investigate their expenditures, not our expenditures? What did my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) say in 1903 when the Boer War was over? He said, through his Minister of Finance, if I recollect correctly, that Canada was responsible for the expenditure of Canada's moneys, but that Canada was not responsible for the expenditure of Imperial moneys. The Shell Committee's expenditures have been expenditures of Imperial moneys, and on the statement of my right hon. friend1, Canada is in no way responsible for the expenditures of the agent of the Imperial Government.
Would it be fair to the Shell Committee to hold an inquiry when it would not be possible for them to make public the instructions which they had received? Reference has been made by the hon. Solicitor General to the Crimean War investigation. What happened in that case? A perfectly futile investigation, with the result that was to be expected. It was not possible, for reasons of State, for the committee to call the witnesses to obtain the evidence which alone would establish the facts, and the result was that the committee was not able to make an investigation nor to make a report, as it vras instructed' to do. The whole investigation was futile, and It would be manifestly unjust to the committee for an inquiry to be 'had into their transactions when it would not be open to obtain the evidence as to what the British War Office had instructed them to do.	.
What is the attitude of this Government with regard to the motion? My right hon. friend the leader of the Government has dealt with this matter, and at page 1591 of Hansard he says:
Now, what course does the Government propose, to take with regard to the motion which my right hon. friend has proposed to this House?
As far as the Shell Committee is concerned_
I shall speak afterwards of another matter-our proposal is this: We shall direct the attention oi the British Government in detail to every charge, allegation and rumour broughlt up 5n this House or elsewhere by my right hon. friend or by any of bis supporters with regard to the Shell Committee. We shall further inform the British Government that if an inquiry is thought advisable we are prepared to co-operate with them to^ the fullest extent, and to issue any commission, take any proceedings, pass any
legislation, and do any other act for the purpose of making that inquiry as full, thorough, and complete as they deem advisable.
Then, further, the .Prime Minister made this statement:
The Shell Committee is one thing; the Government's responsibility in connection with it is another. I thoroughly admit what responsibility we had with regard to the Shell Committee, namely, to appoint men of -good repute, of high character, of experience, of recognized ability, and to co-operate with them so far as in us lay in order that they might do their best to develop the industries of this country for the production of munitions. But there is something else to be said, and I repeat that, if my right hon. friend, or any of Ris followers, has any charge to make against a member of the Government in regard to any of these matters let him make that charge in distinct and understandable terms, and he will have the -investigation as soon as he so desires.
I do not think it necessary to deal particularly with the so-called charge made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley). It was really a condensation of the speech of the hon. member for Garleton. It certainly was not, a charge against the honour, the honesty, or the integrity of any member of this Government. It was a more or less condensed statement of alleged facts and some opinion as to losses alleged to have been sustained through the operations of the Shell Committee.
This evening the matter has been dealt with at some considerable length by my hon. friend from Richmond. He has referred particularly to transactions of the Shell Committee with the two companies in the United States relating to the matter of the fuses. The Shell Committee may have made mistakes in placing the contracts- that is admitted. My hon. friend from Richmond dealt with the incorporation of two companies in the United States. I looked over, rather hurriedly, the agreement which was submitted between the Shell Committee and the Minister of Militia, and one of these companies. It was stated that * an order had been placed for a very large amount,and that an advance had been made of a considerable sum of money-how much,
I have forgotten for the moment,-in prepayment of the contract. It is not an unusual thing to make advance payments to responsible firms where orders for munitions are placed and where large expenditure is required to instal necessary machinery. The Government of Canada, if it placed an order with the Vickers-Maxim Company in England-and I recollect that such an offer was before us for consideration about a year and a half ago-would require to pay one-quarter or one-fifth of the amount of the

contract. The Government pays in advance to the Ross Rifle Company for the rifles which that company were to deliver. I am only mentioning these facts to show that it is not unusual in such contracts to stipulate that payment shall be made in advance. Under section 15 of the agreement-which I have not before me-provision is made for a guarantee by responsible parties to ensure that the company in question would carry out its contract. I do not know at present whether such a guarantee was taken or not, but I think that could be ascertained. And it appears to me that, in so far as the argument of my hon. friend from Richmond was founded upon the provision of the contract that a large sum of money was to be paid over in advance, it may well be that the section of the agreement which provides for a guarantee would protect the Shell Committee. Contracts have been entered into by this Government in which advances have been made, and the guarantee of a responsible guarantee company taken for the purpose of protecting the Government against default on the part of the contracting company.
One further feature was dwelt upon by the hon. member for Richmond. He said that the agreement was approved of by the Minister of Militia, and he drew the inference from that that it was just as if that contract had been -made with the Government of Canada. How did the Minister of Militia sign himself in that agreement. He signed himself as acting for His (Britannic Majesty's Government and not for the Gevernment of Canada. It is perfectly clear, therefore, that . while the Minister of Militia did sign the contract as stated by the hon. member for Richmond, he signed it not on behalf of the Dominion Government, but on behalf of the (Government of the United Kingdom.
Mr. Speaker, it is twenty minutes after twelve o'clock, and, as I have a good deal more to say upon this subject, and would like to look into one or two matters, including this point of the guarantee, I beg to move that the debate he adjourned.

I understood that it had been agreed that the debate was to be concluded to-night; but, of course, if the hon. gentleman wishes to adjourn it, I must admit he has two good reasons-first, he may be tired; and, second, he has a very heavy task before him.
